extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and applicants (practitioners evaluating or drafting nature-based product claims under 35 U.S.C. §101)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent-eligibility of nature-based products and related claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the two-step Alice/Mayo framework, in particular the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis for nature-based product exceptions. Includes examples showing what structural, functional, physical, chemical, and combinatorial changes can render nature-based claims eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 – statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (e.g., composition of matter, manufacture, process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All example analyses begin by confirming Step 1: YES when claims are directed to a statutory category (composition of matter, manufacture, or process). If Step 1 is NO the analysis ends; otherwise proceed to the nature-based product exception analysis (Step 2A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based products, determine whether the claimed subject matter is directed to a judicial exception (product of nature) by assessing whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics it is an exception (Step 2A: YES); if it has such differences, it is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO). The guidance is illustrated across multiple examples (purified small molecules, proteins, nucleic acids, bacteria, mixtures, compositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural differences can show a marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in chemical or physical structure relative to the natural counterpart (e.g., different chemical substitution, removal/addition of groups, altered crystalline form, different glycan) can establish a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 5-methyl amazonic acid (addition of methyl group) and deoxyamazonic acid (hydroxyl replaced by hydrogen) are structural changes that render claims eligible; purified Antibiotic L in tetrahedral crystals or with a high-mannose N-glycan is structurally distinct from the natural form; peptides with ≥90% identity but containing at least one non-natural substitution are structurally different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional differences can show a marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in biological or pharmacological function between the claimed product and its natural counterpart can demonstrate a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 5-methyl amazonic acid stimulates hair growth in addition to treating cancer; recombinant Antibiotic L expressed in yeast has lower immunogenicity and different half-life; genetically modified Pseudomonas containing extra plasmids degrades multiple hydrocarbons. Functional changes rise to the level of a marked difference even if structural changes accompany them or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical or chemical property changes can show a marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Alterations in physical/chemical properties (e.g., solubility, crystalline form, release profile, powder flow, bioavailability) can establish marked differences from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making amazonic acid soluble in water via a solubilizing agent (stable aqueous composition) changes solubility; enveloping amazonic acid core with a natural polymeric layer produces colonic release and improved bioavailability; crystalline form changes (tetrahedral vs hexagonal-pyramidal) change physical behavior and support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations that create a non-natural structure can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims limited to compositions where naturally occurring substances are physically joined into a non-natural structure can have markedly different characteristics and be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a pharmaceutical composition comprising a core of amazonic acid enveloped by a layer of natural polymeric material produces a non-natural structure with different in vivo behavior (colonic release) and thus qualifies as not a product of nature (Step 2A: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims are construed by the structure implied, not limited to process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, product-by-process claims are limited to the structural characteristics of the product implied by the recited steps, not to the recited manipulations themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim 'A composition comprising an acid produced by a process which comprises: providing amazonic acid; and replacing the hydroxyl group...' is interpreted as the product deoxyamazonic acid; if that product is structurally different from the natural counterpart, claim can be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that encompass both natural and non-natural embodiments risk ineligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers embodiments that are identical to natural products as well as changed embodiments may fail the marked difference test because some embodiments will lack marked differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a broad claim to 'Antibiotic L' that encompasses naturally occurring hexagonal-pyramidal crystal form and non-natural tetrahedral crystals is ineligible because at least some embodiments are identical to what exists in nature (Step 2A: YES). Limiting claims to only the non-natural forms can cure eligibility problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere discovery of a natural principle or property is not patentable (aggregation/packaging exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering qualities of natural products or packaging/aggregation of unmodified natural species without altering them does not confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funk Brothers example: selecting mutually non-inhibitive natural strains and packaging them together is tantamount to discovery of handiwork of nature and is ineligible. The combination that produces no change in the species' functions or structure is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims focused on practical application can be eligible without marked-difference analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to a practical application or process of using a nature-based product (e.g., method of treating a disease) can be not directed to the product-exception even though they recite a nature-based product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: methods of treating colon or breast cancer by administering amazonic acid are analyzed as claims focused on a process of practical application and are therefore not directed to the nature-based product exception (Step 2A: NO); the markedly different characteristics analysis need not be applied in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling or chemical linkage that creates a single non-natural molecule can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Attaching a label or chemically linking two components into a single molecule that does not occur in nature results in different structural and functional characteristics sufficient to avoid the product-of-nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an isolated nucleic acid with a fluorescent label attached is a single molecule that is structurally and functionally different (fluorescent) from the natural gene and is eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vectors comprising heterologous sequences create non-natural combinations and can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to vectors that combine a natural nucleic acid with heterologous sequences (sequences not naturally co-occurring in the organism) are limited to non-natural combinations and thus are not products of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a vector comprising SEQ ID NO:1 and a heterologous nucleic acid (e.g., viral promoter) results in different genetic structure/expression and qualifies as not a product of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims limited by sequence identity plus non-natural substitution can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting nucleic acid or peptide claims to sequences having a specified identity to a natural sequence AND containing at least one non-naturally occurring substitution can establish marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims to nucleic acids or peptides with ≥90% identity to a natural sequence but containing at least one substitution not known to occur in nature are treated as structurally different and eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence in nature must be shown to bar eligibility; mere possibility of rare natural occurrence is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner cannot show that the claimed non-natural variant or combination exists in nature, the mere possibility that such a molecule might randomly occur does not render the claim ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Myriad: 'The possibility that an unusual and rare phenomenon might randomly create a molecule similar to one created synthetically through human ingenuity does not render a composition of matter nonpatentable.' Therefore, claim eligibility may stand unless the particular mixture/variant can be shown to exist in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation when analyzing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze claims for eligibility under their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification; interpret claim scope to determine whether it covers natural embodiments or is limited to non-natural variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claim example analyses state they are 'analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation' — examiners should construe claims broadly to determine whether the claim as written encompasses natural products, and then apply Steps 2A/2B accordingly.
